Part I - Physics¶

Part I, Section 1: physical constants and units.

Theory¶

All of Part I is built from five fundamental constants. They are defined once, here, with the values of CODATA 2018 (the SI redefinition of 2019 fixes h, e and c exactly; m_e and eps_0 are measured):

symbol

meaning

value

\(h\)

Planck constant

6.62607015e-34 J s

\(e\)

elementary charge

1.602176634e-19 C

\(m_0\)

electron rest mass

9.1093837015e-31 kg

\(c\)

speed of light

299792458 m/s

\(a_0\)

Bohr radius

5.29177210903e-11 m

(The previous implementation carried three slightly different electron masses and two wavelength formulas. The differences are of order \(10^{-8}\) and have no practical effect, but a single source removes the question.)

Units¶

The simulation works in nanometres for lengths and volts for potentials:

  • lengths and pixel sizes: nm,

  • spatial frequencies: 1/nm,

  • projected potentials: V nm (potential integrated along the beam),

  • interaction parameter: rad / (V nm),

  • angles: rad inside the code (mrad at the user interface),

  • aberration coefficients: nm (as in the notation of Krivanek, see temsim.physics.optics).

Atomic form-factor tables are published in Angstrom; ANGSTROM converts.

Projected potential prefactor¶

The Fourier transform of the electrostatic potential of an atom is proportional to its electron scattering amplitude \(f_e(q)\) (Mott–Bethe, nonrelativistic electron mass; the relativistic mass change enters the interaction parameter, not the potential):

\[\tilde V(q) = \frac{h^2}{2\pi m_0 e}\, f_e(q) \qquad (1.1)\]

With \(f_e\) in Angstrom the prefactor evaluates to 47.878 V Å2 (POTENTIAL_PREFACTOR_V_A2). This is the reciprocal of the constant \(\kappa = 2\varepsilon_0 / (a_0 e)\) that appears in the Bohr-radius form of the literature (and in abTEM); the equality is checked in the tests.

Part I, Section 2: the fast electron.

Theory¶

An electron accelerated through the voltage \(U\) has the kinetic energy \(E = eU\). At 80 kV this is already 16 % of the rest energy, so the relativistic relations are used throughout.

Momentum and wavelength¶

\[p = \frac{1}{c}\sqrt{E^2 + 2 E m_0 c^2}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{h}{p} \qquad (2.1)\]

(wavelength_nm(); 4.18 pm at 80 kV, 2.51 pm at 200 kV.)

Relativistic factor¶

\[\gamma = 1 + \frac{E}{m_0 c^2} \qquad (2.2)\]

Interaction parameter¶

Inside the specimen the electron wave \(\psi\) obeys the Schroedinger equation with the relativistically corrected mass \(\gamma m_0\) and the potential \(V(\mathbf r)\). Within the projection (phase-grating) approximation of Section 4 the wave acquires, per slice, the phase

\[\varphi(x,y) = \sigma\, V_{\mathrm{proj}}(x,y), \qquad \sigma = \frac{2\pi\,\gamma\, m_0\, e\, \lambda}{h^2} \qquad (2.3)\]

with the projected potential \(V_{\mathrm{proj}} = \int V\,dz\). In the units of temsim.physics.constants \(\sigma\) is given in rad/(V nm) (interaction_parameter()); at 80 kV it is 0.0101 rad/(V nm), at 200 kV 0.0073 rad/(V nm).

Part I, Section 3: projected atomic potentials.

Theory¶

From scattering amplitude to potential¶

Tabulated elastic electron scattering amplitudes \(f_e(q)\) (Angstrom, with \(q = |\mathbf q|\) in 1/Angstrom, \(q = 2\sin\theta/\lambda\)) are related to the atomic potential by Eq. (1.1), \(\tilde V(q) = (h^2 / 2\pi m_0 e) f_e(q)\). The multislice method needs the potential projected along the beam, \(V_{\mathrm{proj}}(r) = \int V\,dz\). By the projection-slice theorem its two-dimensional Fourier transform is the central section \(\tilde V(q_x, q_y, 0)\), so

\[V_{\mathrm{proj}}(r) = \frac{h^2}{2\pi m_0 e} \int_0^\infty f_e(q)\, J_0(2\pi q r)\, 2\pi q\, dq \qquad (3.1)\]

(POTENTIAL_PREFACTOR_V_A2 = \(h^2/2\pi m_0 e\)). The tests evaluate this integral numerically and compare with the closed forms below.

Parametrisations¶

Two analytic fits of \(f_e\) are available, selected by name.

Kirkland (E. J. Kirkland, Advanced Computing in Electron Microscopy, 2nd ed., 2010) fits three Lorentzians and three Gaussians,

\[f_e(q) = \sum_{i=1}^{3} \frac{a_i}{q^2 + b_i} + \sum_{i=1}^{3} c_i\, e^{-d_i q^2}.\]

Inserting this into Eq. (3.1) and using \(\int_0^\infty J_0(2\pi q r)\, 2\pi q\, dq/(q^2+b) = 2\pi K_0(2\pi\sqrt b\, r)\) and the Gaussian Hankel transform gives

\[V_{\mathrm{proj}}(r) = \sum_{i=1}^{3}\Big[\, 2\,\alpha_i\, K_0(\beta_i r) + \sqrt{\pi/\delta_i}\;\gamma_i\, e^{-\delta_i r^2}\Big], \qquad (3.2)\]

with the rescaled parameters \(\alpha_i = \pi a_i C\), \(\beta_i = 2\pi\sqrt{b_i}\), \(\gamma_i = \pi^{3/2} c_i\, C / d_i^{3/2}\), \(\delta_i = \pi^2/d_i\), where \(C = h^2/(2\pi m_0 e)\).

Lobato & Van Dyck (Acta Cryst. A 70, 636, 2014) use five terms \(f_e(q) = \sum_{i=1}^{5} A_i (2 + B_i q^2) / (1 + B_i q^2)^2\), which behave correctly at large \(q\) (proper Mott–Bethe asymptotics) and are the better choice for heavy atoms and high scattering angles. The corresponding projected potential is

\[V_{\mathrm{proj}}(r) = 2\sum_{i=1}^{5}\Big[ \frac{2\alpha_i}{\beta_i} K_0(\beta_i r) + \alpha_i\, r\, K_1(\beta_i r)\Big], \qquad (3.3)\]

with \(\alpha_i = \pi^2 A_i C / B_i^{3/2}\) and \(\beta_i = 2\pi/\sqrt{B_i}\).

The parameter tables (103 elements each) are those published with the two papers; they are shipped with the package in temsim/physics/data/ (the files originate from the abTEM distribution, which compiled them from the original publications).

Numerical kernel on a pixel grid¶

Eqs. (3.2) and (3.3) are integrable logarithmic singularities at \(r = 0\) (\(K_0(\beta r) \sim -\ln r\)). Sampling at pixel centres would give a pixel-size dependent, wrong peak value. Two measures keep the sampled kernel a faithful pixel average:

  1. Soft core. Every evaluation uses \(r_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sqrt{r^2 + a^2}\) with \(a = \epsilon\,\Delta\) (\(\Delta\) pixel size, default \(\epsilon = 10^{-3}\)), which removes the singularity without noticeably changing the potential.

  2. Supersampling. Pixels whose centre lies within supersample_radius_px pixels of the atom are replaced by the mean of an \(n\times n\) sub-grid (default \(n = 8\)).

The kernel is returned in V nm with the atom at index [0, 0] (FFT convention), so that convolution with a density map is a product in Fourier space (Section 4).

Thermal motion¶

The tables describe a static atom. Isotropic thermal displacements with root mean square amplitude \(u\) (per direction) smear the potential with a Gaussian, \(V \to V * G_u\), which is a multiplication in Fourier space,

\[\tilde V(k) \to \tilde V(k)\; e^{-2\pi^2 u^2 k^2} \qquad (3.4)\]

(equivalent to \(e^{-B s^2}\) with \(B = 8\pi^2 u^2\), \(s = k/2\)). The area integral is conserved; only the peak is lowered. Eq. (3.4) is baked into the stored spectrum so that it costs nothing at run time (KernelBank).

Part I, Section 5: the displacement (strain) field.

Theory¶

A real 2D crystal is never a perfect lattice: it is rippled, stretched by the substrate and bent around defects. Instead of one free shift per atom (thousands of parameters, hopelessly ill-conditioned) the smooth part of the deformation is described by a displacement field \(\mathbf u(\mathbf r)\), and an atom at \(\mathbf r\) is moved to

\[\mathbf r' = \mathbf r + \mathbf u(\mathbf r) \qquad (5.1)\]

(the per-atom shifts of Part II then describe only what the field cannot).

Parametrisation¶

The field is sampled on a coarse control grid of \(H_c \times W_c\) nodes, which spans the image area \([0, H-1]\times[0, W-1]\) (pixel coordinates, rows first). Node \((i,j)\) sits at

\[\mathbf r_{ij} = \Big(\tfrac{i}{H_c-1}(H-1),\; \tfrac{j}{W_c-1}(W-1)\Big), \qquad (5.2)\]

and carries the two components of \(\mathbf u\) (row direction, column direction). Between the nodes the field is interpolated with a bicubic convolution kernel (Keys with \(a=-1/2\), i.e. Catmull-Rom), which is \(C^1\)-continuous, passes through the node values and reproduces polynomials up to second degree. With the \(t = (n-1)\,r/(N-1)\) coordinate in node units, \(i = \lfloor t\rfloor\), \(f = t - i\), one axis reads

\[u(t) = \sum_{m=-1}^{2} u_{i+m}\, h_m(f), \quad h_{-1} = \tfrac12(-f^3 + 2f^2 - f),\; h_0 = \tfrac12(3f^3 - 5f^2 + 2),\; h_1 = \tfrac12(-3f^3 + 4f^2 + f),\; h_2 = \tfrac12(f^3 - f^2),\]

and the 2D field is the tensor product. The stencil of the outermost cells needs nodes beyond the grid; they are the linear extrapolation of the two outermost nodes (\(u_{-1} = 2u_0 - u_1\)), so that a uniform strain is reproduced exactly up to the image border. Outside the image the coordinate is clamped to the border (constant displacement, no strain there). The interpolation is plain tensor algebra and hence differentiable to any order, which Eq. (5.4) needs (derivative of the strain with respect to the control nodes).

The control tensor has shape (1, 2, Hc, Wc): channel 0 holds the row component, channel 1 the column component.

Strain, rotation, energy¶

With the displacement gradient \(J_{ij} = \partial u_i / \partial r_j\) (computed by automatic differentiation of the interpolation) the small-strain tensor and the local rotation are

\[\varepsilon = \tfrac12 (J + J^{\mathsf T}), \qquad \omega = \tfrac12 (J - J^{\mathsf T}) \qquad (5.3)\]

and the linear isotropic elastic energy density (Lamé parameters \(\lambda, \mu\))

\[w = \tfrac12 \lambda\, (\operatorname{tr}\varepsilon)^2 + \mu\, \varepsilon : \varepsilon. \qquad (5.4)\]

Part II uses \(\langle w\rangle\) over the atoms as a regulariser: it penalises stretching and shearing but not rigid rotation, which belongs to the group transformation. The relation to the trace, \(\operatorname{tr}\varepsilon = \nabla\cdot\mathbf u\), is the local relative area change.

Refining the grid¶

resample_control() re-samples an existing field on a finer or coarser node grid. Because the interpolation passes through the nodes, refining is lossless up to the interpolation error between old nodes; coarsening loses structure the new grid cannot represent.

Reading old states¶

Earlier program versions normalised the point coordinates by the padded image size and sampled the control grid with transposed axes. A saved strain state of that kind is converted by from_legacy_control(), which evaluates the old field at the nodes of the present convention (exact at the nodes; between them the two interpolants differ by the interpolation error only).

Part I, Section 4: atomic structure.

Theory¶

From atoms to a density map¶

A layer \(\ell\) is a set of atoms at positions \(\mathbf r_i\) (pixel coordinates, rows first) with weights \(w_i\). The projected potential of the layer is the superposition of the atomic potentials \(v(\mathbf r)\) (Section 3),

\[V_\ell(\mathbf r) = \sum_i w_i\; v(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i) = (\rho_\ell * v)(\mathbf r), \qquad \rho_\ell(\mathbf r) = \sum_i w_i\,\delta(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i). \qquad (4.1)\]

On the pixel grid the density \(\rho_\ell\) is built by bilinear rasterisation: an atom at \((y, x)\) with \(y = j + f_y\), \(x = i + f_x\) (integer parts \(j, i\), fractions \(f\)) deposits its weight on the four neighbouring pixels with the weights \((1-f_y)(1-f_x)\), \((1-f_y)f_x\), \(f_y(1-f_x)\), \(f_y f_x\). This preserves the total weight and the centre of mass exactly and makes the map differentiable with respect to the positions. The convolution of Eq. (4.1) is a product in Fourier space,

\[\tilde V_\ell(\mathbf k) = \tilde\rho_\ell(\mathbf k)\,\tilde v(\mathbf k), \qquad (4.2)\]

evaluated with real FFTs (rasterise(); the convolution itself lives in temsim.physics.multislice). The grid is padded by a margin so that atoms near the border contribute correctly to the image area; the periodicity of the FFT then wraps only vacuum around. An atom whose rasterisation cell does not lie completely inside the padded grid is dropped.

Atom weights¶

The weight of an atom combines two continuous numbers, both of which can be optimised: the occupancy \(p_i = \sigma(o_i) \in (0,1)\) (logistic of the logit \(o_i\); “is there an atom?”) and the effective atomic number \(Z_i\) (“which atom?”). Two interpretations of \(Z_i\) exist.

Single-element layer. The kernel is that of the layer’s element with reference number \(Z_i^0\) (its start value), and \(Z_i\) scales the amplitude:

\[w_i = \frac{Z_i}{Z_i^0}\; p_i. \qquad (4.3)\]

At the start this is exactly \(p_i\); “from 6 to 7” means “scatters like N instead of C” to first order, without distorting the scale of the whole potential.

Mixed layer (list of elements \(E_1 < E_2 < \dots\) with atomic numbers \(N_1 < N_2 < \dots\)). Here \(Z_i\) selects the element by piecewise linear interpolation (“tent functions”, partition of unity):

\[m_k(Z) = \max\Big(0,\ \min\Big(\tfrac{Z - N_{k-1}}{N_k - N_{k-1}},\ \tfrac{N_{k+1} - Z}{N_{k+1} - N_k}\Big)\Big), \qquad \sum_k m_k(Z) = 1, \qquad (4.4)\]

and the layer is the sum of one density per element, \(\rho_k = \sum_i m_k(Z_i)\, p_i\,\delta(\cdot - \mathbf r_i)\), each convolved with its own kernel. The number of atoms is conserved by the partition of unity, unlike with Eq. (4.3). \(Z\) outside \([N_1, N_{\mathrm{last}}]\) is clamped (gradient zero there).

Rigid group transformation¶

Atoms of one group move together. With the group shift \(\mathbf s\), rotation angle \(\theta\), and per-axis scale \((s_y, s_x)\), about the centre \(\mathbf c = (H/2, W/2)\) of the image area,

\[\begin{split}\mathbf r' = \mathbf c + \mathbf s + S\,R(\theta)\,(\mathbf r - \mathbf c), \qquad R = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{pmatrix}, \quad S = \operatorname{diag}(s_y, s_x). \qquad (4.5)\end{split}\]

The smooth strain field of Section 5 is applied afterwards (transform()). Bounds on \(\mathbf s\), \(\theta\), \(S\) are optimisation constraints and belong to Part II.

Building initial lattices¶

Starting structures come from a lattice recipe (LatticeSpec): a 2D cell with vectors \(\mathbf a_1 = a(1, 0)\), \(\mathbf a_2 = b(\cos\gamma, \sin\gamma)\) and a basis of (element, f_1, f_2, z); atom positions are \(\mathbf R_{mn} + f_1\mathbf a_1 + f_2\mathbf a_2\) for all lattice points \(\mathbf R_{mn} = m\mathbf a_1 + n\mathbf a_2\) covering the image (plus a margin that allows for shifts and rotation of the group), rotated about the image centre and shifted by an offset. Basis atoms with equal height (within 0.01 nm) form one layer. Types: graphene (two C atoms, hexagonal), mx2 (2H dichalcogenide from ase.build.mx2, three layers), custom (explicit basis) and file (any ASE-readable structure, sliced by height).

Part I, Section 6: the multislice method.

Theory¶

Wave equation in the specimen¶

A fast electron with wave function \(\Psi(\mathbf r, z)\) travelling along \(z\) obeys, after separating the fast phase \(\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i z/\lambda}\) and neglecting backscattering (the paraxial / high-energy approximation),

\[\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial z} = \frac{\mathrm i\lambda}{4\pi}\nabla_\perp^2\psi + \mathrm i\sigma\,V(\mathbf r, z)\,\psi, \qquad (6.1)\]

with the interaction parameter \(\sigma\) of Eq. (2.3) and the potential \(V\) in volts. The first term is diffraction (free propagation), the second scattering by the specimen.

Splitting the operators¶

Cutting the specimen into slices of thickness \(\Delta z_j\) and treating the two terms of Eq. (6.1) alternately (a first-order operator splitting; Cowley and Moodie) gives for slice \(j\)

\[\psi_{j}^{+} = t_j\,\psi_j, \qquad t_j(\mathbf r) = \exp\!\big(\mathrm i\sigma V^{\mathrm{proj}}_j(\mathbf r)\big) \qquad (6.2)\]

(the phase grating, \(V^{\mathrm{proj}}_j = \int V\,dz\) over the slice) followed by free propagation over the distance \(\Delta z\) to the next slice, which is a multiplication in Fourier space,

\[\tilde\psi_{j+1}(\mathbf k) = P(\mathbf k;\Delta z)\,\tilde\psi_j^{+}(\mathbf k), \qquad P(\mathbf k;\Delta z) = \exp\!\big(-\mathrm i\pi\lambda\,\Delta z\,|\mathbf k|^2\big). \qquad (6.3)\]

Eq. (6.3) is the paraxial (Fresnel) propagator. Propagators compose, \(P(\Delta z_1)P(\Delta z_2) = P(\Delta z_1+\Delta z_2)\); therefore empty slices need not be visited and the remaining path to the end of the stack is a single propagation (exit_wave()).

Slice order¶

Each layer carries its own height \(z_\ell\). The beam passes the layers in ascending \(z\) for beam_direction = "+z" and in descending \(z\) for "-z"; the propagation distance between two layers is the difference of their own heights (never the distance on the other side). The exit plane is at the height of the last layer in beam direction.

Sampling and aliasing (band limit)¶

On a grid of spacing \(\Delta x\) the highest representable frequency is \(k_N = 1/(2\Delta x)\). The transmission function \(\exp(\mathrm i\sigma V)\) contains harmonics of all orders of the atomic potential; the product with the wave folds frequencies above \(k_N\) back into the band (aliasing). The standard remedy is to restrict the wave to \(|\mathbf k| \le \tfrac23 k_N\) after every transmission (Kirkland, ch. 6): then the products of two band-limited waves fit into the grid again. This is done by setting the propagator to zero outside the disk,

\[P_{\mathrm{bl}}(\mathbf k) = P(\mathbf k)\;\Theta\big(f\,k_N - |\mathbf k|\big), \qquad f = \tfrac23. \qquad (6.4)\]

band_limit = 0 switches the limit off (the behaviour of all earlier versions, and the setting used when legacy files are loaded). Honest remark: for the sparse, weakly scattering specimens of this project the numerical gain could not be demonstrated against a much finer reference (differences stay at the \(10^{-3}\) level with or without the limit); the limit is kept as the textbook default because it guarantees an alias-free wave for strongly scattering or coarsely sampled specimens, and costs nothing inside the retained band.

Projected potential of a slice¶

The potential of a slice is the convolution of the atom density with the atomic kernel, Eq. (4.2). Elements of mixed layers add; a constant offset is removed (the median, a global phase that does not influence intensities but keeps the numbers small), and the result is scaled by the group’s contrast factor \(c_g\):

\[V^{\mathrm{proj}}_\ell = c_{g(\ell)}\Big[\sum_e \rho_{\ell,e} * v_e - \operatorname{median}\Big(\sum_e \rho_{\ell,e} * v_e\Big)\Big]. \qquad (6.5)\]

Part I, Section 7: the objective lens (wave optics).

Theory¶

The exit wave \(\psi_{\mathrm{exit}}(\mathbf r)\) leaves the specimen and passes the objective lens. In the weak-lens, linear-in-the-aberrations picture used throughout, the lens acts in Fourier space (spatial frequency \(\mathbf k\), with the scattering angle \(\alpha = \lambda |\mathbf k|\)) by a multiplication with a transfer function \(T(\mathbf k)\),

\[\tilde\psi_{\mathrm{img}}(\mathbf k) = T(\mathbf k)\,A(\mathbf k)\, \tilde\psi_{\mathrm{exit}}(\mathbf k). \qquad (7.1)\]

Wave aberration¶

Departures of the lens from the ideal are collected in the aberration function, a series in the angle \(\alpha\) and the azimuth \(\varphi\) (Krivanek notation, coefficients \(C_{nm}\) of order \(n\) and multiplicity \(m\)),

\[\chi(\alpha, \varphi) = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \sum_{n,m} \frac{C_{nm}}{n+1}\,\alpha^{\,n+1}\cos\!\big(m(\varphi - \varphi_{nm})\big). \qquad (7.2)\]

The azimuth is measured from the row axis towards the column axis, \(\varphi = \operatorname{atan2}(k_{\mathrm{col}}, k_{\mathrm{row}})\). The orders in use are listed in ABERRATION_TERMS: defocus \(C_{10}\), two-fold astigmatism \(C_{12}\), coma \(C_{21}\), three-fold astigmatism \(C_{23}\), spherical aberration \(C_{30}\), and higher terms. Units: \(C_{10}, C_{12}, C_{21}, C_{23}, C_{32}, \dots\) in nm; \(C_{30}, C_{34}, C_{45}\) in micrometres (they are of the order of millimetres).

Cartesian form. With \(a_{nm} = C_{nm}\cos(m\varphi_{nm})\) and \(b_{nm} = C_{nm}\sin(m\varphi_{nm})\),

\[C_{nm}\cos\!\big(m(\varphi-\varphi_{nm})\big) = a_{nm}\cos m\varphi + b_{nm}\sin m\varphi. \qquad (7.3)\]

Both forms are the same function. The Cartesian one is preferable for optimisation: the gradient with respect to the angle \(\varphi_{nm}\) scales with \(C_{nm}\) and vanishes for small coefficients, whereas \((a, b)\) are well-conditioned everywhere. polar_to_cartesian() and cartesian_to_polar() convert.

Transfer function¶

\[T(\mathbf k) = \big(\sqrt{1-Q^2} - \mathrm i Q\big)\,\mathrm e^{-\mathrm i\chi(\mathbf k)}\, E(\mathbf k), \qquad (7.4)\]

where \(Q\in[0,1]\) is the amplitude contrast (the part of the contrast not caused by the phase of the specimen, e.g. from inelastic losses) and \(E\) the product of the coherence envelopes below.

Aperture¶

The objective aperture \(A(\mathbf k) = 1\) for \(\alpha \le \alpha_{\max}\) and 0 otherwise cuts off high angles.

Envelopes¶

Partial coherence damps high spatial frequencies. Each source gives a Gaussian factor:

  • Chromatic (energy spread \(\Delta E\) of the electrons and chromatic aberration \(C_c\)) gives a spread of defocus \(\Delta f = C_c\,\Delta E / E_0\) (\(E_0 = eU\)):

    \[E_c(k) = \exp\!\big[-(\pi\lambda\,\Delta f\,k^2)^2\big]. \qquad (7.5)\]

    Here \(\Delta E\) is a parameter of this model (half the \(1/e\) width of the focal-spread distribution, see Envelope); it is fitted together with \(C_c\) and need not coincide with the nominal source value.

  • Spatial (finite source or illumination semi-angle \(\beta\) in rad) damps through the gradient of the aberration function,

    \[E_s(k) = \exp\!\Big[-\Big(\frac{\pi\beta}{\lambda}\Big)^2 \big(C_s\lambda^3k^3 + \Delta z\,\lambda k\big)^2\Big] \qquad (7.6)\]

    with defocus \(\Delta z\) and spherical aberration \(C_s\) (both in nm and taken from Eq. 7.2; higher aberrations are neglected in the envelope).

  • Instability (vibration, drift: defocus jitter \(\sigma_z\)): \(E_i(k) = \exp[-(\pi\lambda\sigma_z k^2)^2]\).

  • Detector (optional MTF): \(E_d(k) = \exp[-k^2/(2\sigma_k^2)]\).

The envelope is the product of the enabled factors, clipped to \([0, 1]\).

Part I, Section 8: image formation (TEM and STEM-HAADF).

Theory¶

Conventional TEM (coherent)¶

The exit wave \(\psi_{\mathrm{exit}}\) of Section 6 is transferred by the lens, Eq. (7.1), on the padded grid (the padding absorbs wrap-around of the Fourier method) and cropped to the field of view afterwards,

\[\begin{split}\psi_{\mathrm{img}} = \mathcal F^{-1}\big[T\,A\,\mathcal F\,\psi_{\mathrm{exit}}\big], \qquad I_{\mathrm{TEM}} = \begin{cases}|\psi_{\mathrm{img}}| & \text{signal = amplitude}\\ |\psi_{\mathrm{img}}|^2 & \text{signal = intensity.}\end{cases} \qquad (8.1)\end{split}\]

A detector records the intensity \(|\psi|^2\). All earlier versions of this project compared the amplitude \(|\psi|\) with the measured image; this is kept as the default for old files (tem_signal = "amplitude") because the fitted contrast parameters (Stobbs factors, normalisation) were calibrated with it, and the physically correct intensity is available as an option.

STEM-HAADF (incoherent)¶

A focused probe \(P(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0)\) is scanned over the specimen. The high-angle annular dark-field detector collects electrons scattered between the angles \(\theta_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(\theta_{\mathrm{out}}\). This signal is dominated by thermal diffuse (incoherent) scattering from the individual atoms, so the image is an incoherent convolution of the probe intensity with an object function \(O\),

\[I_{\mathrm{HAADF}}(\mathbf r_0) = \big(|P|^2 * O\big)(\mathbf r_0), \qquad O(\mathbf r) = \sum_{e} \sigma_e\,\rho_e(\mathbf r). \qquad (8.2)\]

Probe. The probe in Fourier space is the aperture times the aberration phase, \(\tilde P(\mathbf k) = A_{\alpha_c}(\mathbf k)\,\mathrm e^{-\mathrm i\chi(\mathbf k)}\) with the convergence semi-angle \(\alpha_c\); its intensity is blurred by the finite size of the electron source (Gaussian of standard deviation \(s\), so \(\exp(-2\pi^2 s^2 k^2)\) in Fourier space) and normalised to unit area,

\[|P|^2 = \Big|\mathcal F^{-1}\tilde P\Big|^2 * G_s,\qquad \sum |P|^2 = 1. \qquad (8.3)\]

The aberration phase \(\chi\) is the same function as in TEM, Eq. (7.2), but with its own (corrected-probe) coefficients.

Object. \(\rho_e\) is the atom density of element \(e\) and \(\sigma_e\) the cross-section for scattering into the detector ring. It is not the projected potential: the integral of the projected potential decreases from B over C and N to O while the HAADF signal grows roughly as \(Z^{1.7}\). Using the elastic scattering factor \(f_e(q)\) (Section 3) and the Einstein model for thermal diffuse scattering with the one-dimensional r.m.s. displacement \(u\), the differential cross-section is \(|f_e|^2\,[1-\exp(-4\pi^2u^2q^2)]\), hence

\[\sigma_e = 2\pi\lambda^2\int_{q_{\mathrm{in}}}^{q_{\mathrm{out}}} |f_e(q)|^2\,\big[1-\mathrm e^{-4\pi^2u^2q^2}\big]\,q\,\mathrm dq, \qquad q = \frac{2\sin(\theta/2)}{\lambda}\approx\frac{\theta}{\lambda}. \qquad (8.4)\]

For \(u=0\) the thermal term vanishes; then the elastic cross-section into the ring is used so that the model does not collapse. (\(q\) in 1/Å, \(f_e\) in Å, \(\lambda\) in Å, \(\sigma\) in Å².)

Part I, Section 9: the complete forward model.

Theory¶

The chain of the preceding sections is evaluated for one state of the specimen (a list of AtomLayer) and one state of the microscope (OpticsState):

\[\text{atoms} \xrightarrow{(4.1),(6.5)} V^{\mathrm{proj}}_\ell \xrightarrow{(6.2),(6.3)} \psi_{\mathrm{exit}} \xrightarrow{(7.4),(8.1)} I_{\mathrm{TEM}}, \qquad \text{atoms} \xrightarrow{(4.1),(8.4)} O \xrightarrow{(8.2)} I_{\mathrm{HAADF}}. \qquad (9.1)\]

Everything is a differentiable tensor operation, so the derivative of any scalar function of the image with respect to atom positions, weights, aberrations or envelope parameters is obtained by back-propagation (Part II).

The simulator owns only fixed quantities (grids, kernels, caches). Parameters enter through the arguments, never as hidden state; the same object therefore serves the full simulation, the training loop and the local window update (temsim.physics.window) without duplicating any physics.

Part I, Section 10: local window update of the image.

Motivation¶

Random seeding (Part II) tries thousands of small changes of the atom set. A change influences the image only within a finite neighbourhood, so re-simulating the whole field of view is wasteful. This section shows that, for the forward model of Sections 6-9, the change of the image can be computed exactly (up to the truncation of kernels) in a small window.

Linearity of the chain¶

STEM. The HAADF image Eq. (8.2) is linear in the atom densities,

\[\Delta I = |P|^2 * \sum_e \sigma_e\,c\,\Delta\rho_e . \qquad (10.1)\]

TEM. Fix all layers but layer \(\ell\). The multislice recursion Eq. (6.2)-(6.3) is linear in the wave (the potentials only enter as multipliers), and so is the lens, Eq. (7.1). If the potential of layer \(\ell\) changes by \(\Delta V\), the wave behind that layer changes by

\[\delta_\ell = \big(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\sigma(V+\Delta V)} - \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\sigma V}\big)\,\psi_\ell, \qquad (10.2)\]

where \(\psi_\ell\) is the (stored) wave entering the layer, and the change travels on linearly through the layers behind it,

\[\delta_{j+1}^{\mathrm{in}} = P(\Delta z_j)\,\delta_j,\qquad \delta_{j+1} = t_{j+1}\,\delta_{j+1}^{\mathrm{in}},\qquad \delta_{\mathrm{img}} = h * \delta_{\mathrm{exit}} \qquad (10.3)\]

(\(h = \mathcal F^{-1}[TA]\) the lens impulse response). All three operators are convolutions with kernels of finite effective range: the propagator spreads a perturbation over \(\lambda k_{\max}\Delta z\), the potential over the atom radius, the lens over the width of \(h\). Truncating each kernel at the radius that contains all but a fraction tail of its energy yields a window of size \(2(\text{extent} + R_V + \sum R_P + R_h)\) in which Eqs. (10.1)-(10.3) are evaluated with FFTs of that window only. The new image is the old image plus the window change; for amplitude signals \(|a+\delta|\), for intensity \(|a+\delta|^2\) with the complex amplitude \(a\).

Compared with earlier versions (one layer, one element, identity group geometry) the restriction is lifted as far as linearity allows:

  • any number of layers, because Eq. (10.3) carries the change through the stack (the stored wave of every layer behind the change is updated on commit);

  • mixed layers: a change is given per element, each with its own kernel;

  • group transformations and strain do not matter here: the caller passes the atoms’ effective positions (before and after), the window only needs where density is added or removed.

Remaining approximations (all removed by refresh): the median subtracted in Eq. (6.5) is kept fixed, kernels are truncated, and changes beyond the support radius are ignored. A change that cannot be handled in a window (propose returns None) is simulated in full by the caller.
